method: Clauset, Shalizi and Newman (2009), SIAM Review 51(4), 661-703
note: p is the share of synthetic datasets from the fitted model that fit it worse than the data does. p below 0.1 rules the power law out; a large p does not rule it in. R is Vuong's normalised log-likelihood ratio: positive favours the power law, negative the rival, and its p above 0.1 means the two cannot be separated at this sample size.

in_degree.label: Origins per destination (in-degree)
in_degree.verdict: Ruled out on its own terms: a power law above 19 produces a fit this poor in 0% of its own draws. The lognormal describes the same tail better. The exponential cannot be separated from it either way.

out_degree.label: Destinations per origin (out-degree)
out_degree.verdict: Not ruled out on its own terms (p = 0.88 over 56 points in the tail), which is a weak thing to be able to say at this size. The lognormal and exponential cannot be separated from it either way.

flight_degree.label: Flight partners per country
flight_degree.verdict: Not ruled out on its own terms (p = 0.15 over 41 points in the tail), which is a weak thing to be able to say at this size. The lognormal and exponential cannot be separated from it either way.

corridor_people.label: People on a corridor
corridor_people.verdict: Ruled out on its own terms: a power law above 126665 produces a fit this poor in 4% of its own draws. The lognormal describes the same tail better.
